{"thought":"Use contradiction with a coprime integer representation, after normalizing the denominator to be positive, and prove the needed parity lemma by contraposition.","actions":[{"type":"finish","query":null,"url":null,"instruction":null,"language":null,"task_id":"initial_classical_proof","title":"Irrationality of \(\sqrt{2}\)","approach":"Classical contradiction using a lowest-terms rational representation and parity.","answer_fragment":"\begin{theorem}
The positive real number \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational. Equivalently, there do not exist integers \(p,q\) with \(q\ne 0\) such that
\[
\sqrt{2}=\frac{p}{q}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose, for contradiction, that \(\sqrt{2}\) is rational. Then there exist integers \(p,q\) with \(q\ne 0\) such that
\[
\sqrt{2}=\frac{p}{q}.
\]
If \(q<0\), replace both \(p\) and \(q\) by \(-p\) and \(-q\), respectively. We may therefore assume that \(q>0\). Dividing \(p\) and \(q\) by their greatest common divisor, we may further assume that the fraction is in lowest terms, so
\[
\gcd(p,q)=1.
\]

We first record the parity fact that if the square of an integer is even, then the integer itself is even. Indeed, let \(n\in\mathbb Z\). If \(n\) were odd, then \(n=2k+1\) for some \(k\in\mathbb Z\), and hence
\[
n^2=(2k+1)^2=4k^2+4k+1=2(2k^2+2k)+1,
\]
which is odd. Thus an integer whose square is even cannot be odd, and therefore must be even.

Squaring \(\sqrt{2}=p/q\) and multiplying by \(q^2\) gives
\[
2q^2=p^2.
\]
Thus \(p^2\) is even. By the parity fact just proved, \(p\) is even, so there exists an integer \(r\) such that \(p=2r\). Substituting this into the preceding equation yields
\[
2q^2=(2r)^2=4r^2.
\]
Dividing by \(2\), we obtain
\[
q^2=2r^2.
\]
Therefore \(q^2\) is even, and the same parity fact implies that \(q\) is even.

Consequently, both \(p\) and \(q\) are divisible by \(2\). Hence \(2\) is a common positive divisor of \(p\) and \(q\), so \(\gcd(p,q)\ge 2\). This contradicts the assumption that \(\gcd(p,q)=1\). Therefore no integers \(p,q\) with \(q\ne 0\) satisfy \(\sqrt{2}=p/q\), and thus \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational.
\end{proof}","confidence":0.99,"assumptions":["Standard facts that every rational number admits a lowest-terms integer representation and that every integer is either even or odd."]}]}
